uses.text: About 88 % of U.S. ammonia (fixed nitrogen) becomes fertiliser, such as urea and ammonium nitrate.
Ammonia is also the starting point for explosives, plastics and synthetic fibres.
Nitrogen gas shields chips and welds from air and pushes crude oil out of wells; liquid nitrogen freezes and preserves biological samples.

hazardStatements.text: Contains gas under pressure; may explode if heated
Contains refrigerated gas; may cause cryogenic burns or injury

hazards.note: Aggregated by PubChem from 1001 reports by companies to the ECHA C&L Inventory; the percentage after a statement is the share of reports that give it. 4.7 % of the reports (47 of 1001) say nitrogen does not meet the GHS hazard criteria.

crust.note: Earth's crust, as given (mg/kg is parts per million by mass).

origin.note: Read off Fig. 39 at the dotted 'age of the Sun' line (t = 9.2 Gyr after the Big Bang, 4.6 Gyr ago): pixel fractions of the stacked areas (agb 0.741, massive_stars 0.259); quantised to 0.05. Stack height 72 px. Cross-check with the paper's text: '74% of N are produced by AGB stars' (figure reading 0.741).

bonding.note: N₂ molecules with a triple bond, one of the strongest bonds known — which is why nitrogen is so unreactive.

air.text: Unreactive; it makes up 78 % of the air. Electric sparks make it combine with oxygen to nitric oxide.

water.text: No reaction with water; slightly soluble.

plantRole.text: Taken up mostly as nitrate or ammonium; part of proteins, nucleic acids and chlorophyll, and, after carbon, the element plants need in the largest amount.

humanRole.text: Part of every amino acid, protein and nucleic acid; obtained from dietary protein.

roles.text: Part of every amino acid and every base of DNA and RNA.
Part of every amino acid and every base of DNA and RNA.
Part of every protein and nucleic acid; one of the six elements found essential in every prokaryote analysed.
Part of every protein and nucleic acid; one of the six elements found essential in every prokaryote analysed.

uptake.text: Nitrate (NO₃⁻) and ammonium (NH₄⁺) from the soil water; legumes also use N₂ from the air, through bacteria in their root nodules

known.text: One of the ten elements recognised as essential in the second half of the 19th century, once plants could be grown in nutrient solutions

deficiency.text: Plants stay small, with narrow, pale green to yellow leaves; the yellowing starts on the older leaves, because the plant moves their nitrogen to the young ones. Cereals form fewer side shoots and fewer grains per ear.

toxicity.text: Too much ammonium as the only nitrogen source harms many plants: leaves yellow, growth stalls and tissue dies. Barley is sensitive to it, rice tolerant; a little nitrate alongside eases the damage.

soil.text: Soil particles do not hold nitrate, so it travels with the soil water and is easily lost. A crop takes up only about half of the fertiliser nitrogen in the first year; the rest stays in the soil or escapes, as nitrate into waters or as ammonia and nitrous oxide into the air.

Factory-made nitrogen fertiliser comes from the Haber–Bosch process, which turns nitrogen from the air into ammonia at high temperature and pressure; it accounts for more than half of the energy used in commercial farming.

partners.text: Only a small group of microbes can turn the air's N₂ into ammonia. Legumes house rhizobia in root nodules; alders, Casuarina, Ceanothus and some 200 other woody plants house Frankia instead, and cycads and the water fern Azolla partner with cyanobacteria.

wild.text: Plants of acid soils and wetlands tend to prefer ammonium, while plants of limy soils prefer nitrate; in acid forest soils, ammonium and amino acids are the main forms of nitrogen on offer.

forest.text: Nitrogen is the nutrient that limits most temperate forests, many boreal ones and some tropical ones; trees get it from nitrate and ammonium released as soil organic matter decays.

Without nitrogen-fixing plants a forest gains less than a kilogram of fixed nitrogen per hectare a year; with them, up to several hundred. Alders always carry their nodules, Ceanothus shrubs not always.

food.text: Good nitrogen supply, with part of it given late in the season, raises the gluten proteins in wheat grain and so its baking quality; durum wheat for pasta is wanted with more than 12–13 % protein.

Leafy vegetables such as spinach, lettuce and chard, and beetroot, can store a lot of nitrate, and food safety authorities set upper limits for spinach and lettuce; avoiding excess fertiliser and choosing the time of harvest keep levels down.

levels.note: Table 2.20. Low: 20–25; high: above 35. The table gives no excess class for nitrogen.

levels.part: leaves at the base of new shoots

isotopeUses.text: Bacteria grown on heavy nitrogen-15 and then moved to ordinary nitrogen-14 made DNA of intermediate density, separable in a centrifuge: Meselson and Stahl's 1958 proof that DNA is copied semi-conservatively.

The share of nitrogen-15 differs between nitrogen sources and changes as nitrogen passes through soils, plants and food webs, so it traces where the nitrogen in an ecosystem comes from and where it goes.

environment.text: Nitrogen from fertilisers and sewage that washes into rivers, lakes and coastal seas feeds blooms of algae (eutrophication), which use up the oxygen in the water as they decay.

history.nameOrigin: From the French nitrogène, built from the Greek nitron ('native soda', i.e. nitre) and -genes ('producing'), because it is a constituent of nitre.
history.note: Scheele, Cavendish and Priestley were studying the same unbreathable residue of air at about the same time.

prose.text: Nitrogen is a colourless, unreactive gas that makes up most of the air we breathe, yet it is also a building block of every protein and every strand of DNA. Plants cannot use the gas directly, because the triple bond holding the two atoms of N₂ together is extraordinarily strong; legumes such as peas and clover solve this by housing bacteria in root nodules that turn it into ammonia. A nitrogen atom, [He] 2s² 2p³, has three 2p electrons, one in each p orbital with parallel spins (ground term ⁴S°₃/₂). This half-filled subshell is so stable that nitrogen's first ionisation energy, 1402 kJ/mol, exceeds oxygen's 1314 kJ/mol.
